canonical_title: The Preserving Machine and Other Stories
author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: Dick's first major hardcover story collection (Ace, 1969), taking its title from a fable about a machine built to preserve music as living creatures, which mutate into something wild and unrecognizable.
page_summary:
The Preserving Machine and Other Stories is an early collection (Ace Books, 1969) and one of the first substantial gatherings of Dick's short fiction between hard covers. The title story imagines a machine that converts musical scores into animals so the music can survive a coming collapse of civilization; the creatures escape into the wild and evolve into savage, unrecognizable forms, and the preserved music comes back altered and strange.

That fable of preservation-as-mutation is characteristically Dickian: an attempt to fix and protect something stable produces instead transformation and loss of control. The surrounding stories, drawn largely from his 1950s magazine work, carry his familiar figures—robots and automata, realities that come apart, the human element that persists or fails to persist under pressure.

As one of the collections that established Dick's reputation as a short-story writer, it matters for showing the range he had already achieved by the late 1960s, and for its title metaphor, which reads as a wry parable about art, entropy, and the impossibility of keeping anything exactly as it was.
